The four discrete editing actions are ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, and NOOP: ADD writes a new entry; UPDATE rewrites or merges an existing entry; DELETE removes an entry contradicted by new evidence or outdated; and NOOP means no update is made because the information is already covered or unimportant for long-term memory [2602.06052#s45.p1].

HippoRAG uses an LLM to transform a corpus into a schemaless knowledge graph that serves as an "artificial hippocampal index," mimicking the neocortex's processing of perceptual input [2405.14831#s2.p5]. On this graph it runs the Personalized PageRank (PPR) algorithm, seeding it with the query's key concepts to explore KG paths and identify relevant subgraphs, effectively performing multi-hop reasoning in a single retrieval step [2405.14831#s2.p5]. More broadly, HippoRAG synergistically orchestrates LLMs, knowledge graphs, and PPR to mimic the roles of neocortex and hippocampus [2405.14831#s1.p1], combining LLMs' KG construction abilities with the retrieval advantages of structured knowledge for more effective RAG [2405.14831#s20.p1].

The append-only structure is the **Immutable Episodic Log** (denoted $\mathcal{K}_{\text{ledger}}$), which acts as the operational source of truth and enables asynchronous reconciliation/rollback [2603.11768#s22.p1]. It is paired with a mutable active graph in the dual-track substrate [2603.11768#s22.p1], and reconciliation replays/corrects memory against this immutable ledger [2603.11768#s23.p10].
According to the paper, semantic memories in NornicDB's three-tier cognitive decay model receive a 69-day half-life [2604.11364#s2.p2].

When new evidence arrives, CUPMem treats it as a potential state update and makes an explicit write-side adjudication about older memories rather than merely appending the new evidence to a retrieval pool [2605.06527#s15.p1]. An LLM-based adjudicator evaluates each candidate old state and decides whether it should remain active, be archived as `STALE`, be replaced, or be marked unresolved (KEEP/STALE/REPLACE/UNKNOWN), giving new evidence write-side authority to revise, retire, or block older assumptions before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. If an old item is invalidated its state is written as `STALE`; if only the old default's unsafety can be established, the slot is marked `UNKNOWN_CURRENT` [2605.06527#s64.p19]. All such modifications obey a temporal causality constraint: only later evidence may revise or archive earlier memory items [2605.06527#s64.p19]. The design principle is conflict-targeted write-side revision, so new evidence triggers explicit decisions about older states that may no longer be usable [2605.06527#s62.p1].

The two papers' headline results conflict as follows. In the preregistered comparison, the LLM-compiled wiki scored higher than single-round RAG on LLM-judged synthesis criteria, though at about 21× the per-query LLM-token use [2605.18490#s52.p1][2605.18490#s1.p1]. As for the key factor, the preregistered paper attributes the disagreement to how retrieval is done and what is measured: a decomposition-retrieval variant of RAG closed about 94% of the `inter_paper_mapping` gap [2605.18490#s45.p1], came within 0.4 points of the wiki on both criteria at ~3.4× lower per-query token use [2605.18490#s52.p1], and the paper frames its contribution as showing *why* such comparisons disagree [2605.18490#s2.p1]. It also notes that compiled-knowledge architectures have been compared against retrieval baselines "with materially different results depending on how the compiled knowledge is served and what is measured" [2605.18490#s2.p1]. WiCER's own framing of its result as a reversal tied to corpus scale (80 documents per topic) is stated in the passage, but the context does not explicitly name a single key explanatory factor for the cross-paper disagreement beyond the serving/measurement dependence noted above.

HippoRAG 2 uses its knowledge graph to aid the retrieval process rather than to expand the retrieval corpus itself, which introduces less LLM-generated noise [2502.14802#s5.p3]. It leverages the PPR algorithm over an explicitly constructed open knowledge graph [2502.14802#s5.p4]. In contrast, the LLM Wiki compiles the corpus offline into a persistent cross-linked markdown wiki (entities, concepts, sources, and analyses with cross-references), and at question time a tool-using agent lists and reads pages rather than retrieving raw chunks [2605.18490#s13.p1][2605.18490#s2.p1]. The wiki is described as an LLM-built version of the compiled abstractive memory family with a markdown-rendered intermediate representation [2605.18490#s7.p1].

When new evidence arrives, CUPMem treats it as a potential state update and makes an explicit write-side adjudication about older memories: an LLM-based adjudicator evaluates each candidate old state and decides whether it should remain active, be archived as `STALE`, be replaced, or be marked unresolved (`KEEP`/`STALE`/`REPLACE`/`UNKNOWN`) [2605.06527#s15.p1]. This gives new evidence write-side authority to revise, retire, or block older assumptions before query time [2605.06527#s15.p1]. If an old item is invalidated its state is written as `STALE`; if only the old default is shown unsafe but no replacement is settled, the slot is marked `UNKNOWN_CURRENT` [2605.06527#s64.p19]. All such modifications obey a temporal causality constraint: only later evidence may revise or archive earlier memory items [2605.06527#s64.p19]. Invalidation is not limited to the directly touched slot—CUPMem expands the search to structurally affected state regions via topology-triggered belief propagation [2605.06527#s15.p1]. At query time, active items serve as current grounding, stale items are treated as historical context, and unresolved slots prevent an unsafe old default from being used as a premise [2605.06527#s15.p1].

ReFind adds an agent-controlled iterative retrieval loop with chat-specific controls (reformulation, local expansion, session fusion, temporal filtering, deduplication) over a BM25 index of the raw text, deferring representation decisions to query time [2608.12888#s38.p1][2608.12888#s9.p1]. So the key difference is agent-controlled, multi-round query formulation versus a single-shot static retrieve-and-rerank pipeline.

Agent Zero Memory treats a knowledge update as a new, timestamped belief recorded alongside its evidence rather than a destructive overwrite, so the most-recent fact is recoverable with its provenance and the superseded fact remains distinguishable from its correction [2608.29606#s21.p1]. Its timeline makes "when" and "what changed" first-class, so a superseded fact is distinguished from its correction rather than returned stale [2608.29606#s10.p1], and nothing is destructive: events accumulate rather than replacing one another, every item carries provenance, and a correction updates belief without erasing what was held [2608.29606#s3.p8]. The emphasized design principle is that quality is retrieval-dominated and governed by the structure and provenance of retrieved memory rather than a model's parametric knowledge [2608.29606#s21.p2][2608.29606#s10.p1].

Raw-RAG instead challenges the presumed necessity of explicit memory mutation, arguing that capable readers can resolve dynamic states from sufficient raw history and that disabling mutation improves accuracy in the tested configuration [2610.30755#s2.p10]. It emphasizes evidence access and coverage: retrieving answer values does not ensure sufficient supporting paths, and complete-store access does not close the gap to raw evidence [2610.30755#s2.p10], with Raw-RAG offsetting lower utilization through high coverage [2610.30755#s15.p4][2610.30755#s15.p6].
